screens.title: Introduction to Relational Databases and SQL Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you will gain a clear mental model of relational databases and how S Q L lets you define and query structured data. Relational databases organize data into tables made of rows and columns. Each row is a complete record, and each column stores a specific attribute. You will learn why keys — primary and foreign — matter for correctness and how S Q L's DDL and DML let you build and then manipulate those tables. Practical commands include CREATE TABLE to define structure, INSERT INTO to add rows, and SELECT to retrieve data. We will walk through a real Employees example and a hands-on Customers and Orders activity that ties the ideas together. Along the way I will point out common mistakes, like forgetting quotes around string or date literals, and show how choosing correct data types prevents waste and errors. By the end you should be able to design simple related tables, create them with DDL, insert sample rows, and write SELECT queries to verify your data. Now let's explore key topics so you know what to practice next.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Introduction
Introduction to Relational Databases and SQL
Build tables, enforce relationships, and run queries with declarative SQL.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

This chapter teaches how to model structured data using tables, how primary and foreign keys link records, and how to use basic SQL to define, insert, and retrieve data. Expect terminal-style code examples for CREATE TABLE, INSERT INTO, and SELECT, plus a small hands-on design exercise.

Why it matters: reliable data structure and correct queries are the foundation of analytics, reporting, and downstream data pipelines.

Tables
Rows and columns that store structured records like a spreadsheet.
Keys
Primary and foreign keys link data and ensure integrity across tables.
SQL
A declarative language to define, insert, and query data safely.
Explore Key Topics
Schema Design
Choose columns, keys, and data types to match your data and queries.
DDL & DML
Use CREATE TABLE, INSERT, and SELECT to build and inspect data.
Hands-on Lab
Create Customers and Orders, insert rows, and run verification queries.
Concept Visual
Customers
CustomerID, FirstName, LastName, Email
Orders
OrderID, CustomerID (FK), OrderDate, TotalAmount
Tip: primary keys uniquely identify rows. Foreign keys point to those keys to express real-world relationships.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus your practice so you gain practical, verifiable skills. First, you will be able to explain core relational database concepts: how tables, rows, columns, primary keys, and foreign keys represent structured information and relationships. A concrete example is a Customers table with CustomerID that uniquely identifies each customer and an Orders table that uses CustomerID as a foreign key. Second, you will understand S Q L's role: S Q L is a declarative language for defining structures and querying data. You will learn the difference between DDL for creating structures and DML for operating on rows. Third, you will write basic DDL commands such as CREATE TABLE, specifying columns and constraints, and modify schemas when necessary. Finally, you will execute essential DML commands like INSERT and SELECT to add and retrieve data. Each objective includes a small practice milestone so you can confirm competency by creating tables, inserting sample rows, and running select queries to verify relationships.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Verification
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives page explains how to practice and verify your skills. You will write CREATE TABLE statements to define columns, data types, and constraints, then insert sample rows and run SELECT queries to view the results. For each milestone, pick a small dataset: for example, three customers and four orders. After creating tables, insert rows and then run SELECT * FROM Customers and SELECT * FROM Orders to verify storage. A useful verification step is to select specific columns, such as SELECT FirstName, LastName, Salary FROM Employees, which confirms both data correctness and data types. When practicing, pay attention to common mistakes: string and date literals must be in single quotes; numeric values must not be quoted; primary keys must be unique and not null. These checks help you discover schema or insert-time errors quickly. Treat schema design like a contract between producers and consumers of the data — if you define columns and types well, downstream queries and pipelines are more reliable.

screens.title: Tables, Rows, and Columns
screens.narratorSegment: A relational table is a collection of rows and columns that together represent a set of records. Think of a table as a spreadsheet where each row is a single record and each column is an attribute describing every record. For example, a Customers table could have columns CustomerID, FirstName, LastName, Email, and RegistrationDate. Each row holds one customer's values for those columns. This structure matters because it sets expectations: columns define the type and meaning of data, and rows represent concrete instances. A common misconception is to treat a table like an unstructured log. In relational design, the schema enforces types and constraints, which protects downstream queries and analytics from dirty or inconsistent data. Concrete example: if CustomerID is an integer primary key, every row must have a unique integer in that column; it is wrong to insert text there or to leave it null. Practical takeaway: design columns with clear names and appropriate data types so code and analysts can rely on the contract your table provides. Question to consider: when you see a dataset, what columns would you choose to make records complete and queryable?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Tables store structured records; columns define attributes and types; rows are individual entries that conform to the schema.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Tables, Rows & Columns
What is a table?
A table is a relation: columns declare the type and meaning of each attribute, and rows are records that fill those columns. A consistent schema makes queries predictable.
Columns
Named attributes like CustomerID, Email, or RegistrationDate that each carry a data type.
Rows
Individual entries. Each row provides values for every column in the schema.
Key Takeaway

Treat the table schema as a contract. Good names and types reduce errors and surprise in queries.

Concrete example: Customers table
Columns
  • CustomerID (INT)
  • FirstName (VARCHAR)
  • LastName (VARCHAR)
  • Email (VARCHAR)
  • RegistrationDate (DATE)
Misconception: a table is not simply a JSON blob store. Relational tables expect consistent columns and typed values, which enable indexing, joins, and reliable queries.
Try this
When you inspect a dataset, ask which column uniquely identifies rows and which columns describe attributes you will query most often.

screens.title: Primary and Foreign Keys
screens.narratorSegment: Primary and foreign keys are the mechanism that makes relationships reliable in a relational database. A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table—no two rows can share the same primary key value and the primary key must not be null. For example, EmployeeID or CustomerID are typical primary keys. A foreign key is a column in one table that references the primary key in another table to establish a relationship. For instance, Orders. CustomerID can be a foreign key that points to Customers. CustomerID, indicating who placed the order. This prevents orphan records—orders that do not belong to any existing customer. A common misconception is to think a foreign key is required for every link; in practice you add foreign keys where you need enforced referential integrity. Concrete example: If you try to insert an order with a CustomerID that does not exist in Customers and the foreign key constraint is enforced, the database rejects the insert. Takeaway: use primary keys to guarantee uniqueness and foreign keys to express and enforce real-world relationships. Primary and Foreign Keys means primary keys ensure uniqueness; foreign keys express referential integrity between tables and prevent orphaned records.. In practical terms, how relationships and uniqueness are enforced. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Primary & Foreign Keys
Primary Key
A column or set of columns that uniquely identifies each row. Must be unique and not null.
Example
EmployeeID INT PRIMARY KEY in an Employees table guarantees each employee has a single identifier.
Common Mistake
Using a non-unique column as a primary key or allowing nulls undermines identity and causes duplicate record ambiguity.
Foreign Key
A column that references a primary key in another table to establish a relationship and maintain integrity.
Example
Orders table has CustomerID that references Customers.CustomerID so every order links to an existing customer.
Pro Tip

Add foreign key constraints where data integrity matters; omit them in high-throughput pipelines only when performance or replication patterns demand it.

screens.title: SQL: DDL, DML, and DCL
screens.narratorSegment: S Q L is organized into sublanguages that express different intentions. Data Definition Language, or DDL, contains commands that define or modify database structures. CREATE TABLE is the most important DDL command for this chapter; it declares column names, data types, and constraints like primary keys or unique constraints. Data Manipulation Language, DML, contains commands to operate on actual rows: INSERT adds rows, SELECT retrieves them, UPDATE changes existing rows, and DELETE removes rows. Data Control Language, DCL, handles permissions and is important in production but outside this initial chapter's hands-on practice. A common misconception is that S Q L is imperative; instead S Q L is declarative: you state what you want, like selecting rows that match a condition, and the database decides the execution plan. Concrete example: use CREATE TABLE to build an Employees table, then use INSERT INTO to add rows and SELECT to verify what you added. Takeaway: separate schema design (DDL) from row operations (DML) and practice both so you can create durable tables and populate them safely. SQL: DDL, DML, and DCL means use ddl to define structure and dml to manipulate rows; dcl manages permissions and is used in later administration topics.. In practical terms, which sql commands define structure and which manage data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › SQL Sublanguages
DDL
CREATE, ALTER, DROP
Define and modify schemas. Example: CREATE TABLE Employees (...).
DML
INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE
Operate on rows. Example: INSERT INTO Employees (...) VALUES (...);
DCL
GRANT, REVOKE
Manage permissions. Relevant later for production databases.
Declarative vs Imperative
SQL is declarative: you state the result you want. The engine chooses an execution plan. Misconception: writing SQL is not like scripting each step; focus on the results and let the database optimize.

screens.title: CREATE TABLE: Defining Columns and Types
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a CREATE TABLE example to make schema design concrete. The statement defines a table name and a parenthesized list of columns with data types and optional constraints. For example, the Employees table example uses EmployeeID INT PRIMARY KEY, FirstName and LastName as VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, Email as VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE, HireDate as DATE, and Salary as DECIMAL(10, 2). The primary key enforces uniqueness; NOT NULL ensures required fields; UNIQUE prevents duplicate emails. Data types matter: use DATE for dates so the engine can index and compare chronologically, and DECIMAL for precise monetary values. A common mistake is choosing overly large VARCHAR lengths by default; this wastes storage and can hide design issues. Concrete example: CREATE TABLE Employees (EmployeeID INT PRIMARY KEY, FirstName VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, LastName VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, Email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE, HireDate DATE, Salary DECIMAL(10, 2)); After creating the table, inspect the schema in your client to confirm types and constraints. Takeaway: map each real-world attribute to a precise S Q L type and constraint so the database can enforce the rules you expect. CREATE TABLE: Defining Columns and Types means define each column with a suitable data type and constraints; prefer precise types for clarity and efficiency.. In practical terms, a code walkthrough of a basic employees table. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Define each column with a suitable data type and constraints; prefer precise types for clarity and efficiency.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › CREATE TABLE Walkthrough
Employees table example
Below is the canonical CREATE TABLE example used in this chapter. Use it as a template for defining primary keys, NOT NULL fields, UNIQUE constraints, and precise numeric types for money.
CREATE TABLE Employees (
  EmployeeID INT PRIMARY KEY,
  FirstName VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
  LastName VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
  Email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE,
  HireDate DATE,
  Salary DECIMAL(10, 2)
);
Explanation
  • EmployeeID INT PRIMARY KEY: unique identifier, non-nullable by design.
  • VARCHAR(n): variable-length string with maximum n characters; prefer realistic limits.
  • DECIMAL(10, 2): precise numeric type for financial values with two decimals.
Key Takeaway
Choose types deliberately. Constraints like PRIMARY KEY, NOT NULL, and UNIQUE are your first defense against bad data.

screens.title: INSERT INTO: Adding Rows and Common Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Inserting data uses INSERT INTO followed by the table, optional column list, and VALUES. The values must match the column order and types declared in the schema. For example, INSERT INTO Employees (EmployeeID, FirstName, LastName, Email, HireDate, Salary) VALUES (1, 'Alice', 'Smith', 'alice. smith@example. com', '2022-01-15', 75000.00); Note how string and date literals are enclosed in single quotes while numeric values are not. A frequent mistake is forgetting quotes around strings or dates, which produces syntax errors. Another error is mismatching the number of columns and values or inserting a NULL into a NOT NULL column. The example also shows UNIQUE constraints on Email; inserting a duplicate email will fail. Use explicit column lists in INSERT statements to make your intent clear and robust to schema changes. Practice inserting multiple rows and then run SELECT to verify the inserted data. Takeaway: match types and column order, quote strings and dates, and respect constraints to avoid runtime errors. INSERT INTO: Adding Rows and Common Mistakes means provide values that match the declared columns and types; quote strings and dates, leave numbers unquoted, and respect not null and unique constraints.. In practical terms, how to insert data safely and avoid syntax errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › INSERT INTO
Example INSERT statements
INSERT INTO Employees (EmployeeID, FirstName, LastName, Email, HireDate, Salary)
VALUES (1, 'Alice', 'Smith', 'alice.smith@example.com', '2022-01-15', 75000.00);

INSERT INTO Employees (EmployeeID, FirstName, LastName, Email, HireDate, Salary)
VALUES (2, 'Bob', 'Johnson', 'bob.j@example.com', '2021-06-01', 82000.50);

INSERT INTO Employees (EmployeeID, FirstName, LastName, Email, HireDate, Salary)
VALUES (3, 'Charlie', 'Brown', 'charlie.b@example.com', '2023-03-10', 68000.00);
Errors to watch for
  • Forgetting single quotes around strings and dates causes syntax errors.
  • Mismatching column count and values will be rejected by the engine.
  • Violating UNIQUE or NOT NULL constraints results in insertion failure.
Common Mistake

Writing INSERT INTO Employees VALUES (3, John, Doe, ...); without quotes around John causes an error. Always use single quotes for string and date literals.

screens.title: SELECT Queries: Retrieving Data
screens.narratorSegment: Retrieving data is the most common activity you will perform. The simplest query is SELECT * FROM TableName; which returns all columns and rows. This is useful for an initial inspection, but SELECT * can return more data than you need and may be inefficient in production. A better pattern for routine checks is SELECT FirstName, LastName, Salary FROM Employees; which returns only the columns you care about and is simpler to read. Column-specific selects reduce bandwidth, make results clearer, and allow you to rely on known column order in client code. A frequent misconception is that SELECT * is always acceptable during development. While it is convenient, it can hide schema changes and lead to brittle code when columns are added or reordered. Concrete example: after inserting three employee rows, run SELECT * FROM Employees; to see everything, then run SELECT FirstName, LastName, Salary FROM Employees; to validate specific attributes like pay. Takeaway: use SELECT * for quick inspection but prefer explicit column lists in scripts and applications to maintain stability. SELECT Queries: Retrieving Data means use select * for quick inspection; prefer explicit column lists for clarity, efficiency, and robustness in scripts and applications.. In practical terms, select * vs column-specific selects and why both are useful. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › SELECT Queries
Quick inspection
-- Retrieve all columns and rows
SELECT * FROM Employees;

-- Retrieve specific columns
SELECT FirstName, LastName, Salary FROM Employees;
Why prefer explicit columns?
  • Reduced bandwidth and clearer results for callers.
  • Protects scripts from schema changes like added or reordered columns.
  • Makes intent explicit for reviewers and maintainers.
Check Your Understanding

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Customers & Orders Lab
Starter SQL
-- Step 1: Create Customers table
CREATE TABLE Customers (
  CustomerID INT PRIMARY KEY,
  FirstName VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
  LastName VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
  Email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE,
  RegistrationDate DATE
);

-- Step 2: Create Orders table
CREATE TABLE Orders (
  OrderID INT PRIMARY KEY,
  CustomerID INT,
  OrderDate DATE,
  TotalAmount DECIMAL(10, 2),
  FOREIGN KEY (CustomerID) REFERENCES Customers(CustomerID)
);
Insert & Verify
Insert at least three customers and four orders, making sure Order.CustomerID matches an existing CustomerID. Then run SELECT * on both tables to verify.
-- Insert example customer
INSERT INTO Customers (CustomerID, FirstName, LastName, Email, RegistrationDate)
VALUES (1, 'Ava', 'Green', 'ava.green@example.com', '2022-08-01');

-- Verify data
SELECT * FROM Customers;
SELECT * FROM Orders;

Practice creating schemas, inserting rows, and running selects to confirm referential integrity and data correctness.

screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize three essential ideas to carry forward. First, relational databases store structured data in tables made of rows and columns; design column names and types to reflect the real attributes you will query. Third, S Q L is the declarative language that separates schema definition from data manipulation: use DDL like CREATE TABLE to define structure and DML like INSERT and SELECT to add and retrieve rows. fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you will gain a clear mental model of relational databases and how S Q L lets you define and query structured data. Relational databases organize data into tables made of rows and columns. Each row is a complete record, and each column stores a specific attribute. You will learn why keys — primary and foreign — matter for correctness and how S Q L's DDL and DML let you build and then manipulate those tables. Practical commands include CREATE TABLE to define structure, INSERT INTO to add rows, and SELECT to retrieve data. We will walk through a real Employees example and a hands-on Customers and Orders activity that ties the ideas together. Along the way I will point out common mistakes, like forgetting quotes around string or date literals, and show how choosing correct data types prevents waste and errors. By the end you should be able to design simple related tables, create them with DDL, insert sample rows, and write SELECT queries to verify your data. Now let's explore key topics so you know what to practice next.

These objectives focus your practice so you gain practical, verifiable skills. First, you will be able to explain core relational database concepts: how tables, rows, columns, primary keys, and foreign keys represent structured information and relationships. A concrete example is a Customers table with CustomerID that uniquely identifies each customer and an Orders table that uses CustomerID as a foreign key. Second, you will understand S Q L's role: S Q L is a declarative language for defining structures and querying data. You will learn the difference between DDL for creating structures and DML for operating on rows. Third, you will write basic DDL commands such as CREATE TABLE, specifying columns and constraints, and modify schemas when necessary. Finally, you will execute essential DML commands like INSERT and SELECT to add and retrieve data. Each objective includes a small practice milestone so you can confirm competency by creating tables, inserting sample rows, and running select queries to verify relationships.

This second objectives page explains how to practice and verify your skills. You will write CREATE TABLE statements to define columns, data types, and constraints, then insert sample rows and run SELECT queries to view the results. For each milestone, pick a small dataset: for example, three customers and four orders. After creating tables, insert rows and then run SELECT * FROM Customers and SELECT * FROM Orders to verify storage. A useful verification step is to select specific columns, such as SELECT FirstName, LastName, Salary FROM Employees, which confirms both data correctness and data types. When practicing, pay attention to common mistakes: string and date literals must be in single quotes; numeric values must not be quoted; primary keys must be unique and not null. These checks help you discover schema or insert-time errors quickly. Treat schema design like a contract between producers and consumers of the data — if you define columns and types well, downstream queries and pipelines are more reliable.

A relational table is a collection of rows and columns that together represent a set of records. Think of a table as a spreadsheet where each row is a single record and each column is an attribute describing every record. For example, a Customers table could have columns CustomerID, FirstName, LastName, Email, and RegistrationDate. Each row holds one customer's values for those columns. This structure matters because it sets expectations: columns define the type and meaning of data, and rows represent concrete instances. A common misconception is to treat a table like an unstructured log. In relational design, the schema enforces types and constraints, which protects downstream queries and analytics from dirty or inconsistent data. Concrete example: if CustomerID is an integer primary key, every row must have a unique integer in that column; it is wrong to insert text there or to leave it null. Practical takeaway: design columns with clear names and appropriate data types so code and analysts can rely on the contract your table provides. Question to consider: when you see a dataset, what columns would you choose to make records complete and queryable?

Primary and foreign keys are the mechanism that makes relationships reliable in a relational database. A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table—no two rows can share the same primary key value and the primary key must not be null. For example, EmployeeID or CustomerID are typical primary keys. A foreign key is a column in one table that references the primary key in another table to establish a relationship. For instance, Orders. CustomerID can be a foreign key that points to Customers. CustomerID, indicating who placed the order. This prevents orphan records—orders that do not belong to any existing customer. A common misconception is to think a foreign key is required for every link; in practice you add foreign keys where you need enforced referential integrity. Concrete example: If you try to insert an order with a CustomerID that does not exist in Customers and the foreign key constraint is enforced, the database rejects the insert. Takeaway: use primary keys to guarantee uniqueness and foreign keys to express and enforce real-world relationships. Primary and Foreign Keys means primary keys ensure uniqueness; foreign keys express referential integrity between tables and prevent orphaned records.. In practical terms, how relationships and uniqueness are enforced. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

S Q L is organized into sublanguages that express different intentions. Data Definition Language, or DDL, contains commands that define or modify database structures. CREATE TABLE is the most important DDL command for this chapter; it declares column names, data types, and constraints like primary keys or unique constraints. Data Manipulation Language, DML, contains commands to operate on actual rows: INSERT adds rows, SELECT retrieves them, UPDATE changes existing rows, and DELETE removes rows. Data Control Language, DCL, handles permissions and is important in production but outside this initial chapter's hands-on practice. A common misconception is that S Q L is imperative; instead S Q L is declarative: you state what you want, like selecting rows that match a condition, and the database decides the execution plan. Concrete example: use CREATE TABLE to build an Employees table, then use INSERT INTO to add rows and SELECT to verify what you added. Takeaway: separate schema design (DDL) from row operations (DML) and practice both so you can create durable tables and populate them safely. SQL: DDL, DML, and DCL means use ddl to define structure and dml to manipulate rows; dcl manages permissions and is used in later administration topics.. In practical terms, which sql commands define structure and which manage data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through a CREATE TABLE example to make schema design concrete. The statement defines a table name and a parenthesized list of columns with data types and optional constraints. For example, the Employees table example uses EmployeeID INT PRIMARY KEY, FirstName and LastName as VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, Email as VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE, HireDate as DATE, and Salary as DECIMAL(10, 2). The primary key enforces uniqueness; NOT NULL ensures required fields; UNIQUE prevents duplicate emails. Data types matter: use DATE for dates so the engine can index and compare chronologically, and DECIMAL for precise monetary values. A common mistake is choosing overly large VARCHAR lengths by default; this wastes storage and can hide design issues. Concrete example: CREATE TABLE Employees (EmployeeID INT PRIMARY KEY, FirstName VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, LastName VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, Email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE, HireDate DATE, Salary DECIMAL(10, 2)); After creating the table, inspect the schema in your client to confirm types and constraints. Takeaway: map each real-world attribute to a precise S Q L type and constraint so the database can enforce the rules you expect. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Inserting data uses INSERT INTO followed by the table, optional column list, and VALUES. The values must match the column order and types declared in the schema. For example, INSERT INTO Employees (EmployeeID, FirstName, LastName, Email, HireDate, Salary) VALUES (1, 'Alice', 'Smith', 'alice. smith@example. com', '2022-01-15', 75000.00); Note how string and date literals are enclosed in single quotes while numeric values are not. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Retrieving data is the most common activity you will perform. The simplest query is SELECT * FROM TableName; which returns all columns and rows. This is useful for an initial inspection, but SELECT * can return more data than you need and may be inefficient in production. A better pattern for routine checks is SELECT FirstName, LastName, Salary FROM Employees; which returns only the columns you care about and is simpler to read. Column-specific selects reduce bandwidth, make results clearer, and allow you to rely on known column order in client code. A frequent misconception is that SELECT * is always acceptable during development. While it is convenient, it can hide schema changes and lead to brittle code when columns are added or reordered. Takeaway: use SELECT * for quick inspection but prefer explicit column lists in scripts and applications to maintain stability.
